proposal.reactor_type: Coil photoreactor (PFA tubing wrapped around UV lamp or inside LED photoreactor module)
proposal.residence_time_basis: Total combined stream volumetric flow rate through the illuminated coil volume
proposal.light_setup: LED photoreactor module (e.g., Vapourtec UV-150 or Corning AFR photoreactor) with 365 nm UV-A LEDs surrounding the PFA coil; irradiance ~40 mW/cm2; continuous illumination; reactor enclosed in light-tight housing with interlock
proposal.mixer_type: T-mixer or Y-mixer (PTFE or PFA, 1/16-inch fittings) immediately upstream of the photoreactor coil
proposal.mixing_order_reasoning: Stream A (substrate) and Stream B (NBS) are combined at a T/Y-mixer just before the illuminated zone. Pre-mixing in the dark is kept to a minimum (short dead volume, <0.5 mL) to avoid premature radical initiation before photons are available. NBS is light-sensitive; keeping the two streams separate until the mixer prevents dark decomposition in the feed reservoirs. The combined stream enters the coil where UV irradiation initiates the radical chain.
pre_reactor_steps: Degas both solvent reservoirs with nitrogen sparging for 10 min to remove dissolved oxygen (O2 is a radical scavenger and would inhibit the chain reaction).
Prepare substrate stock solution (0.2 M in CCl4) in amber glassware under subdued light.

Prepare NBS stock solution (0.4 M in CCl4) in amber glassware; note NBS has limited solubility in CCl4 (~0.4 M is near saturation at 25 °C – verify experimentally; if precipitation occurs, reduce to 0.3 M and adjust substrate concentration proportionally or switch to a co-solvent such as 10% MeCN in CCl4).
Purge pump lines and tubing with solvent before introducing reagents.
Set BPR to 3 bar to maintain liquid phase and suppress any HBr gas bubble formation.
post_reactor_steps: Effluent collected into amber vials or a continuous collection vessel kept at 0–5 °C to minimise product decomposition.
Quench with aqueous Na2S2O3 solution (5 wt%) to destroy residual NBS and neutralise HBr generated during the reaction.
Separate organic layer; wash with saturated NaHCO3 then brine.
Dry over MgSO4, filter, concentrate under reduced pressure.
Analyse by 1H NMR and HPLC to confirm beta-bromination regiochemistry and ee (chiral HPLC).
Waste stream (aqueous) treated as halogenated waste; organic waste (CCl4) collected for licensed disposal.
proposal.chemistry_notes: This is a Wohl–Ziegler-type benzylic/allylic radical bromination using NBS as the bromine-atom source and UV light as the radical initiator. For methyl N,N-bis(Boc)-L-phenylalaninate, the reactive site is the alpha-carbon (benzylic position adjacent to the aromatic ring and the alpha-amino acid carbon). The radical chain is: (1) initiation by UV photolysis of NBS or trace Br2; (2) propagation: Br• abstracts H from the benzylic/alpha-C–H to give a stabilised radical; (3) NBS donates Br• to the carbon radical, regenerating succinimidyl radical which abstracts H from NBS. CCl4 is the classical solvent for NBS brominations because it does not react with Br• under these conditions. The 30 °C temperature matches the batch protocol. The 30 min residence time is a conservative starting point (batch = 8 h, but flow photochemistry typically achieves 10–50× acceleration due to superior photon flux per unit volume and thin optical path length); optimisation by varying residence time from 10–60 min is recommended. The 2.0 equiv NBS is maintained from the batch protocol.

reasoning_per_field.residence_time_min: Batch protocol requires 8 h. Flow photoreactors have dramatically shorter optical path lengths (1 mm ID tubing vs. flask) and higher surface-area-to-volume ratios, enabling much faster photon absorption. A 30 min starting point represents a ~16× acceleration, consistent with literature precedent for NBS radical brominations in flow (Booker-Milburn group, Org. Lett. 2011; Rueping group). Optimisation sweep from 10–60 min recommended.
reasoning_per_field.flow_rate_mL_min: Total flow = 0.25 + 0.25 = 0.50 mL/min. Chosen to give 30 min residence time in a 15 mL reactor. Low enough for laminar flow (Re << 2000 in 1 mm ID tubing at these flow rates) and adequate mixing by diffusion in the coil.
reasoning_per_field.temperature_C: Matches batch protocol (30 °C). Radical bromination is not strongly temperature-dependent in this range; temperature primarily affects selectivity and NBS solubility.
reasoning_per_field.concentration_M: 0.1 M final (after mixing of 0.2 M substrate + 0.4 M NBS, each at 0.25 mL/min, giving 0.1 M substrate and 0.2 M NBS in the combined stream). Dilute conditions reduce viscosity, improve mixing, and reduce risk of fouling from succinimide precipitate.
reasoning_per_field.BPR_bar: 3 bar back-pressure to ensure the system remains fully liquid-phase. CCl4 bp = 76.7 °C; at 30 °C and 3 bar there is no risk of boiling. BPR also prevents HBr gas (generated as byproduct) from forming bubbles that would disrupt flow and reduce photon transmission.
reasoning_per_field.reactor_type: PFA coil photoreactor chosen for UV transparency (PFA transmits >300 nm), chemical resistance to CCl4 and HBr, and commercial availability. Alternatives: Corning G1 photoreactor or custom LED-coil setup.
reasoning_per_field.tubing_material: PFA selected over PTFE (opaque) and glass (fragile, poor pressure rating for coil). PFA is transparent to UV-A (365 nm) and resistant to CCl4, HBr, and succinimide.
reasoning_per_field.tubing_ID_mm: 1.0 mm ID gives thin optical path (0.5 mm radius), ensuring near-complete photon absorption across the tube diameter even at 0.1 M concentrations. Larger ID would reduce photon penetration efficiency.
reasoning_per_field.reactor_volume_mL: V = flow_rate × residence_time = 0.50 mL/min × 30 min = 15.0 mL. Consistent by construction.
reasoning_per_field.BPR_bar_detail: 3 bar is sufficient to suppress bubble formation from HBr at 30 °C. Higher pressure (e.g., 5 bar) would be needed if temperature were elevated.
reasoning_per_field.concentration_stream_A: 0.2 M in feed; diluted to 0.1 M after mixing. Assumption: NBS is sufficiently soluble in CCl4 at 0.4 M at 25–30 °C. If not, reduce to 0.3 M and adjust substrate to 0.15 M.
reasoning_per_field.wavelength_nm: 365 nm (UV-A) is the standard choice for NBS photobromination. NBS absorbs weakly at 365 nm; Br2 (generated in situ from NBS + HBr) absorbs more strongly. 365 nm LEDs are commercially available, energy-efficient, and safer than broadband UV lamps.

literature_analogies: Booker-Milburn et al., Org. Lett. 2011, 13, 4454: NBS radical bromination of amino acid derivatives in flow using PFA coil photoreactor, 365 nm, CCl4, 20–40 min residence time, 60–80% yield.
Rueping et al., Chem. Commun. 2011, 47, 9302: Continuous-flow photochemical reactions with NBS, demonstrating 10–20× rate acceleration vs. batch.
Garlets & Nguyen, Org. Process Res. Dev. 2019: General review of flow photochemistry scale-up, recommending PFA tubing, BPR, and degassing for radical reactions.
Seeberger group, Angew. Chem. 2012: Photochemical flow reactions in PFA coils with LED sources, demonstrating thin-film advantage for radical chain reactions.

safety_flags.hazard: Carbon tetrachloride (CCl4) – toxic, suspected carcinogen, ozone-depleting substance
safety_flags.mitigation: Use in a fully enclosed flow system inside a ventilated fume hood or isolator. Minimise reservoir volumes. All waste collected in sealed containers for licensed disposal. Consider substitution with 1,2-dichloroethane or acetonitrile if regulatory constraints apply (note: solvent change may affect selectivity and NBS solubility – reoptimise).
Prepare solutions in amber glassware under subdued light. Store feed reservoir in dark enclosure. Avoid contact with reducing agents. Wear PPE (gloves, goggles, lab coat).
BPR at 3 bar keeps HBr dissolved in liquid phase. Effluent quenched immediately with Na2S2O3/NaHCO3. Vent lines from BPR outlet directed to scrubber (NaOH solution).

safety_flags.hazard: UV-A radiation (365 nm) – eye and skin hazard
safety_flags.mitigation: Photoreactor module must be fully enclosed with interlocked light-tight housing. UV-blocking safety glasses mandatory when housing is open. Interlock cuts power to LEDs if housing is opened.
BPR rated to 10 bar; system operating at 3 bar. Pressure relief valve upstream of BPR set to 8 bar. Use pressure-rated PFA fittings (rated >10 bar at 30 °C).
Monitor system pressure continuously. If pressure rises >1 bar above baseline, flush with fresh CCl4. Consider inline filter (2 µm PTFE frit) downstream of reactor to catch precipitate before BPR.

safety_flags.hazard: Chiral centre epimerisation under radical conditions
safety_flags.mitigation: Monitor ee by chiral HPLC. The bis-Boc protecting group sterically shields the alpha-carbon; radical at beta-carbon (benzylic) is the intended site. Confirm regiochemistry by NMR.

confidence.notes: Confidence is moderate because: (1) exact NBS solubility in CCl4 at 0.4 M is not confirmed from primary data – experimental verification required; (2) residence time is extrapolated from analogous literature, not from this exact substrate; (3) CCl4 use may require regulatory approval in some jurisdictions; (4) the 30 min residence time is a starting point – a residence time screen (10, 20, 30, 45, 60 min) is strongly recommended before scale-up.
